Malmivuo & Plonsey, bem.fi Ch. 7 (http://www.bem.fi/book/07/07.htm)

checked_sources: Henze et al. 2000 full text PDF (mirror at typeset.io of J Neurophysiol 84:390-400); Europe PMC abstract
evidence_location: Results, paragraph on extracellular spike amplitude vs. distance from the soma (Fig. 6A-C); restated in Discussion ('extracellular spikes can be revealed as far as 140 µm from the cell body')
quote: distances >140 μm from the soma (Fig. 6C), no extracellular spike activity could be distinguished from the background noise
bibliographic_issues: None. Authors, journal, volume 84(1), pages 390-400, year 2000 and DOI all match.

checked_sources: Łęski et al. 2013 full text (Europe PMC XML, PMC3715549)
Lindén et al. 2011 abstract only (Europe PMC); Cell/ScienceDirect full text could not be opened
evidence_location: Łęski 2013: Results, 'simplified model' derivation around Eqs. 4-5 (variances vs amplitudes); Results paragraph on Fig. 6D-F (saturation for uncorrelated input, no saturation for correlated input, citing ref [34] = Lindén 2011). Lindén 2011: abstract.
quote: In the case of uncorrelated input this amounts to simply adding the variances of the single-cell LFPs
discrepancy: The '∝ √N' / '∝ N' wording is the claim's paraphrase: Łęski states that for uncorrelated input variances add, whereas for fully correlated input the PSD 'is found by adding the single amplitudes, not variances'. The non-saturation statement ('the power of the population signal no longer seems to saturate as the population radius increases [34]') is made for correlated input and attributed to Lindén 2011, whose abstract agrees (uncorrelated: radius of a few hundred µm; correlated: set by the spatial extent of correlated activity). Lindén full text not verified.
bibliographic_issues: None. Both citations (PLoS Comput Biol 9(7):e1003137; Neuron 72(5):859-872) match Europe PMC records.

checked_sources: Buzsáki, Anastassiou & Koch 2012, author manuscript at PMC4907333 (fetched via pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)
evidence_location: Section 'Gap junctions and neuron–glia interactions' (under contributors to extracellular fields)
quote: the glial syncytium may contribute to slow and infraslow (<0.1 Hz) field patterns
discrepancy: Source says glia 'may contribute' to slow and infraslow (<0.1 Hz) patterns; it does not say 'only'. The exclusivity is the claim's addition (the review elsewhere only describes the field as spanning 'fast action potentials to the slowest fluctuations in glia'). First half ('Membrane potential changes in non-neuronal cells, such as glia, may also give rise to Ve') is supported.
suggested_fix: …but the glial syncytium is thought to contribute mainly to slow and infraslow (<0.1 Hz) field patterns.
bibliographic_issues: None. Nat Rev Neurosci 13(6):407-420, 2012, DOI 10.1038/nrn3241 match.

checked_sources: Oostendorp et al. 2000 abstract (Europe PMC)
McCann et al. 2019 full text (Europe PMC XML, PMC6708046)
Akhtari et al. 2002 abstract (Europe PMC)
Hoekema et al. 2003 abstract (Europe PMC)
evidence_location: Oostendorp: abstract ('about 0.015 S/m', ratio 1:1/15:1). McCann: Table 3 (Whole skull weighted mean 0.0160 S/m; text and abstract round this to 0.02 ± 0.02). Akhtari: abstract (spongiform 16.2-41.1, top compact 5.4-7.2, lower compact 2.8-10.2 mS/m). Hoekema: abstract (32-80 mS/m, five patients).
quote: Both methods revealed a skull conductivity of about 0.015 [S]/m … a ratio of 1:1/15:1 was found
discrepancy: Minor: 'compact 3-10 mS/m' merges Akhtari's two compact layers (top 5.4-7.2, lower 2.8-10.2 mS/m). McCann's 0.016 S/m is the Table 3 weighted mean (0.0160); the paper's abstract/text quote it rounded as 0.02 ± 0.02 S/m.
suggested_fix: …and 2.8-10.2 mS/m (compact; upper layer 5.4-7.2, lower 2.8-10.2)…; optionally 'weighted mean 0.016 S/m (reported as 0.02 ± 0.02 S/m in the abstract)'.
bibliographic_issues: None. All four citations (IEEE TBME 47(11):1487-1492; Brain Topogr 32(5):825-858; Brain Topogr 14(3):151-167; Brain Topogr 16(1):29-38) match Europe PMC records.

checked_sources: Fam et al. 2018, PMC6239876 (fetched via pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)
evidence_location: Abstract (mean/min/max) and Results (mean 0.36 mm, SD 0.16, SEM 0.04; specimen site; exclusion of case 20)
quote: Mean, minimum, and maximum skull base dural thickness in our study was 0.36, 0.27, and 0.46 mm
discrepancy: Numbers match, but: 20 decedents were enrolled and one was excluded (oblique sectioning), so 19 were analysed; only one site was sampled (dura over the right petrous apex), not the skull base generally; within-specimen variability was large (min-max difference up to 0.45 mm). Convexity dura was not measured, as the claim correctly implies.
suggested_fix: Cranial dura thickness measured at autopsy over the petrous apex (skull base; 19 of 20 decedents analysed) averaged 0.36 mm (0.27-0.46 mm, SD 0.16 mm)…
bibliographic_issues: Title is wrong: the published title is 'Skull Base Dural Thickness and Relationship to Demographic Features: A Postmortem Study and Literature Review' (not 'a cadaveric study and review of the literature'). Journal, 79(6):614-620, 2018 and DOI 10.1055/s-0038-1651501 are correct.

checked_sources: Muthukumaraswamy 2013 full text (Europe PMC XML, PMC3625857)
Goncharova et al. 2003 abstract (Europe PMC)
evidence_location: Muthukumaraswamy: Abstract and Introduction ('~20–300 Hz'); section on muscle physiology ('bandwidth of 20–300 Hz', citing Criswell 2011); section on neuromuscular-blockade studies ('contamination … started around 20 Hz'); section on spectral characteristics ('~1000 fT and 100 μV … less than 20 fT and 1 μV', citing Herrmann & Demiralp 2005). Goncharova: abstract.
quote: The contamination of the frequency spectrum started around 20 Hz … can be ~1000 fT and 100 μV
discrepancy: All numbers are in Muthukumaraswamy (a review; the 20-Hz onset comes from Whitham et al.'s paralysis studies of resting EEG, the 100 µV / <1 µV figures from Herrmann & Demiralp 2005, and 20-300 Hz is the general surface-EMG band for striated muscle, with facial muscles extending to 600 Hz and frontalis starting ~15 Hz). Goncharova's own abstract characterises cranial EMG differently: 'broad frequency distribution from 0 to >200 Hz', peaks 20-30 Hz frontal and 40-80 Hz temporal, and EMG detectable near the vertex above 12 Hz (above 8 Hz in some individuals) even at 15% contraction — i.e. contamination from active contraction can start below 20 Hz.
suggested_fix: Optional: 'Surface EMG spans about 20-300 Hz (Goncharova: 0 to >200 Hz, peaking at 20-30 Hz frontally and 40-80 Hz temporally); contamination of resting EEG begins at about 20 Hz, and with voluntary contraction from ~12 Hz'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Front Hum Neurosci 7:138 (2013) and Clin Neurophysiol 114(9):1580-1593 (2003) match.

checked_sources: Texas Instruments ADS1299-x datasheet SBAS499C (July 2012, revised January 2017), PDF from ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ads1299.pdf
evidence_location: p.1 Features; Section 7.5 Electrical Characteristics (Analog Inputs, DC Channel Performance, AC Channel Performance); Table 4 'Input-Referred Noise … Normal Mode, 5-V Analog Supply and 4.5-V Reference', gain 24 row for 250 SPS
quote: Input-Referred Noise: 1 μVPP (70-Hz BW); Input Bias Current: 300 pA; CMRR: –110 dB
discrepancy: None of substance. Details: 1 µVPP is the typical figure (0.01-70 Hz, gain 24, 250 SPS; max 1.35 µVPP at 25 °C, 1.6 over temperature); Table 4 gives 0.14 µVRMS / 0.98 µVPP at 250 SPS with a 65-Hz −3-dB bandwidth at gain 24; CMRR −110 dB min, −120 dB typ at 50/60 Hz; DC input impedance 1000 MΩ typ with no lead-off (500 MΩ with 6-nA current-source lead-off); input capacitance 20 pF typ; input bias current ±300 pA.
suggested_fix: Optional precision: '1 µV peak-to-peak typical (1.35 µV max) … 1000 MΩ DC input impedance with lead-off detection disabled'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Document number SBAS499C and 2017 revision date match; title matches.

checked_sources: Rosell et al. 1988 abstract (Recercat repository record, recercat.cat/handle/2072/193091); Europe PMC record (bibliographic only). Full text (core.ac.uk PDF) was blocked.

bibliographic_issues: None. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng 35(8):649-651, 1988, DOI 10.1109/10.4599 match.

evidence_location: Chi 2010: Section III.A 'Dry Electrodes'. Lopez-Gordo 2014: Section 1 (Introduction, '5 to 15 KΩ within 5 hours', citing ref [5]) and Section 4.1 ('impedance of the dry electrodes remained constant during 5 hours', wet rising ~2 kΩ/h, same ref [5]).

discrepancy: Supported, but both halves are secondary reports: Chi attributes the 'few minutes' statement to its ref [16]; Lopez-Gordo's 5→15 kΩ in 5 h and dry-constant-over-5-h figures both come from Lin et al. 2011 (IEEE TBME 58:1200-1207, dry polymer foam electrodes).

checked_sources: Ryynänen et al. 2004 abstract (Europe PMC)
Lantz et al. 2003 abstract (Europe PMC)
evidence_location: Ryynänen: abstract (three-layer spherical model; 'as the measurement noise increases the advantage of dense electrode systems is decreased'; 16-mm spacing ≈ 256 electrodes with low realistic noise; 'always beneficial to have at least 64'). Lantz: abstract, Methods/Results (123 electrodes down-sampled to 63 and 31; 9/14 and 11/14).
quote: In 9/14 patients, the distance from the EEG source to the lesion was significantly smaller with 63 than with 31
discrepancy: None in the numbers. 'improved most from 31 to 63' is an inference from 9/14 (31→63) vs. 2 further patients (63→123); Lantz's wording is 'increasing the number of electrodes to 123 increased this number of patients from 9 to 11'. Ryynänen's 64-electrode statement is qualified 'In clinical measurement environments'. Full texts not opened.
bibliographic_issues: None. IEEE TBME 51(9):1547-1554 (2004) and Clin Neurophysiol 114(1):63-69 (2003) match.

checked_sources: Antelis et al. 2013 full text (Europe PMC XML, PMC3629197)
evidence_location: Abstract; Introduction (last paragraph); Results, 'Evaluation of whether the decoding model performance is above chance level'; Discussion
quote: a systematic statistical analysis revealed that these results were not above the chance level
discrepancy: Minor omission: the empirical chance level was estimated both by randomly assigning recorded velocity profiles to EEG of other trials (shuffling) and by randomly generated synthetic EEG/velocity data; the claim mentions only the random pairing.
